checkpoints: Core principle: page on the symptom users actually feel (e.g. checkout failure rate rising, latency crossing a threshold, mass request errors), not the internal cause — a symptom always corresponds to real user harm, so paging on it is always worth waking someone up.

Cause (e.g. high CPU, a pod restart, a queue at 80%) is an internal state that can be completely normal — high CPU can just mean efficient resource utilization, a pod restart can be part of a planned rolling deploy, a queue at 80% can still be within the system's designed operating threshold.

Paging on cause creates constant false alarms because these internal states occur hundreds of times per day during entirely normal operations (autoscaling, rolling updates, periodic batch jobs) with no user harm — this is exactly how 40 pages a night happens.

This produces a 'cry wolf' effect: once false pages repeat enough, on-call starts muting everything, including the one time there's a real incident, because nothing distinguishes trustworthy from noisy alerts anymore.

Cause information is still valuable, but that value belongs to diagnosis, not alarming/paging — preserve it by attaching cause as context/annotation directly on the symptom alert (e.g. listing current CPU/queue depth as likely suspects the moment a checkout-latency page fires) or surfacing it on a standing, non-paging dashboard; cause should never be its own independent alerting channel.

A signal should only page if it meets all three criteria: urgent (can't wait until the next morning), actionable (there's a specific thing on-call can do right now, not just 'now I know'), and real (reflects genuine user harm, doesn't self-heal after a few seconds of flapping); missing any one means it should be a non-urgent ticket or a dashboard line, not a page.

Bug: the formula divides two raw COUNTER values directly (`http_requests_total{status!~"5.."}` / `http_requests_total`) — counters are cumulative totals since the process started, not a measurement over any specific time window.

The formula contains no `[30d]` or any range vector at all, despite the rule name `checkout:sli_availability:ratio30d` implying a 30-day window — so it actually computes the lifetime ratio, not the last 30 days; "ratio over the process's entire history" and "ratio over a 30-day window" are two entirely different quantities, and the rule's name promises the windowed one while the formula computes the lifetime one.

This explains why the SLI stays ~100%: over a long-running service's history, the accumulated successful traffic vastly outweighs a few hours of 5xx errors from one incident last week, so the overall ratio barely moves even though the incident was severe to real users at the time.

Fix: wrap both numerator and denominator in `sum(increase(...[30d]))`, where `increase()` returns the number of increments within a specific window (similar to `rate()` but without dividing by seconds) — matching what the rule name promises, and `sum()` aggregates across instances/labels.

Effect of the fix: a 5xx incident occurring within the 30-day window now directly pulls down the numerator, correctly reflecting how much that incident affects the SLI (unlike before, where it was diluted across the process's entire lifetime).
Verify step: simulate a period with a spike in 5xx error traffic and confirm the 30-day SLI drops clearly in response, in contrast to the old formula which barely reacted to a new incident.
Nêu đúng công thức burn rate = (1 - SLI) / (1 - SLO).
Giải thích đúng ý nghĩa mẫu số: với SLO 99.9%, (1 - SLO = 0.001) chính là error budget được phép trong window SLO (30 ngày).
Giải thích đúng ý nghĩa tử số: (1 - SLI) là tỉ lệ lỗi THỰC TẾ đo được trong window đang xét (1h hoặc 6h), không phải đo trên cả 30 ngày.
Diễn giải đúng con số: burn rate = 14.4 nghĩa là đang tiêu ngân sách nhanh gấp 14.4 lần tốc độ 'vừa đủ cạn sau 30 ngày', tức cả tháng ngân sách sẽ cạn trong khoảng 30/14.4 ≈ 2 ngày.
Viết đúng rule fast-burn: expr `(1 - checkout:sli_availability:ratio1h) / 0.001 > 14.4`, `for: 2m`, `severity: critical` (page ngay lập tức).
Viết đúng rule slow-burn: expr `(1 - checkout:sli_availability:ratio6h) / 0.001 > 3`, `for: 15m`, `severity: warning` (không page, chỉ mở ticket).

Giải thích đúng lý do fast-burn chọn window ngắn (1h) + threshold cao (14.4x): để bắt outage nghiêm trọng nhanh nhất có thể; `for: 2m` chỉ nhằm lọc spike thoáng qua, không phải một phần của việc chọn window/threshold.

Giải thích đúng lý do slow-burn chọn window dài (6h) + threshold thấp (3x): bắt kiểu suy giảm chậm nhưng KÉO DÀI mà một threshold tĩnh đơn lẻ (vd error rate > 1%) dễ bỏ sót, vì tại một thời điểm riêng lẻ tỉ lệ lỗi có thể chưa đủ cao để vượt ngưỡng.
Reframe "blameless": it does not mean nobody is accountable — it is an information-gathering strategy, not a moral exoneration.
If the involved engineer fears discipline, they will hide exactly the most important information: what they did and what they were thinking at the moment of the decision.

That hidden information is the key to understanding why a competent engineer still made a decision leading to the incident — usually a system weakness (missing warning before a dangerous operation, outdated runbook, a confusing CLI interface) rather than personal incompetence.

Postmortem structure includes objective, quantifiable early sections: a Timeline of timestamped events without judgmental language (e.g. "14:03 – deployed X", not blaming a named engineer), and a measurable Impact section with concrete numbers (failed requests, revenue affected, whether the SLA was breached).

Postmortem structure includes a system-level Root cause — not stopping at "engineer X typed the wrong command" but digging one layer deeper to ask why the system allows one mistake to cause such large consequences, and what confirmation/canary/staged-rollout step is missing.
Postmortem structure includes concrete Action items with a clear owner and deadline, not vague promises like "we'll be more careful."

Separate the VP's "who caused this" request into two tracks: the public technical postmortem serves system-level learning without naming individuals critically, while any genuine suspicion of repeated intentional or negligent behavior is handled in a separate private management review — never mixed into the same public document, since mixing destroys blamelessness for future incidents.

The business decision is to activate a pre-agreed error budget policy — freezing high-risk feature releases and shifting team priority to reliability work until the budget recovers, turning the error budget into a real business decision-making tool rather than a static dashboard number.

group_by: ['pod'] is the wrong grouping key because the `pod` label value is different for every one of the 30 failing Pods, so each Pod automatically falls into its own separate group — equivalent to no grouping at all, producing 30 independent alert groups.

group_wait: 0s removes Alertmanager's buffering mechanism — normally group_wait makes Alertmanager wait a short time after a group's first alert to see if other alerts belonging to the same group are about to arrive so they can be merged into one notification; with 0s the first alert is sent immediately with no wait.
The two bugs compound: alerts are not grouped correctly (30 separate groups) AND are sent immediately with no buffer, so the result is exactly 30 separate notifications piling up within seconds.
Fix group_by away from a per-instance identity label (`pod`) to a label reflecting the shared ROOT INCIDENT — use `node`, since all 30 failing Pods sit on the same node that had the network failure.
Combine `node` with `alertname` in group_by (i.e. group_by: ['alertname', 'node']) so that different alert types firing on the same node don't get incorrectly merged into a single group.

Fix group_wait back to a nonzero buffer (e.g. 30s) so Alertmanager has time to gather all 30 near-simultaneous alerts belonging to the same group before sending one aggregated notification instead of one per alert.
Also increase group_interval (e.g. to 5m instead of a very short value) to avoid re-sending too frequently if additional alerts join the same group afterward.

Result of the fix: on-call receives exactly ONE notification (e.g. "30 PodCrashLooping alerts on node X") listing all affected Pods in a single payload — still enough information to know it's a node-level incident, without the overwhelm of 30 consecutive notifications.
Not right away — HPA cannot function until `resources.requests.cpu` is set on the container.

CPU-based HPA (`type: Resource`, `target.type: Utilization`) computes `currentUtilization = (average actual CPU used per pod) / requests.cpu × 100%` — `requests.cpu` is the denominator of that formula.
Without that denominator, HPA has nothing to divide by: `kubectl get hpa` shows TARGETS as `<unknown>/50%` indefinitely.
Consequence: the HPA sits idle and never scales even when real CPU usage spikes, because it literally cannot 'read' utilization without requests.
The fix: add `resources.requests.cpu` (e.g. `100m`) to the container.
`limits.cpu` is good practice too (a ceiling so one pod can't eat the whole node's CPU), but it is NOT the HPA denominator — only `requests.cpu` feeds the utilization formula.
After adding requests, reapply the Deployment then the HPA, and confirm via `kubectl get hpa` that TARGETS shows a real number (e.g. `1%/50%`) instead of `<unknown>` before trusting the HPA to work.
App exposes a cumulative request counter (e.g. `http_requests_total`) via a `/metrics` endpoint — a running total since pod start, NOT requests/second.
Prometheus scrapes that endpoint periodically and stores the metric as a time series.

`prometheus-adapter` (installed via Helm, configured via a rule YAML) is the bridge component between Prometheus and HPA — it exposes computed metrics on the `custom.metrics.k8s.io` API, distinct from the `metrics.k8s.io` API that metrics-server uses for CPU/memory.
In the adapter's rule config, `seriesQuery` declares which Prometheus series exist (e.g. matching on `http_requests_total`).
`resources.overrides` maps Prometheus labels (`pod`/`namespace`) to Kubernetes resources so the computed metric attaches to the correct pod.

`metricsQuery` (e.g. `sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m])) by (pod)`) is the actual PromQL run at query time, converting the cumulative counter into an instantaneous requests/second via a 1-minute rate window.
`name.as` renames the query result (e.g. to `http_requests_per_second`) — this is the exact name HPA must reference.

HPA references the metric by declaring `metrics[].type: Pods`, `pods.metric.name` matching the adapter's name exactly, and `target.type: AverageValue` with `averageValue: "10"` (average per pod) — unlike `Utilization` (a percentage), which is only usable for CPU/memory.
States that the HPA itself is not the bug — it behaved correctly, scaling up in response to sustained high CPU and staying within the maxReplicas:50 ceiling.
Cites the concrete diagnostic step: `kubectl describe pod` on a Pending pod shows a `FailedScheduling` event with `Insufficient cpu`.
Correctly identifies the root cause as a node-capacity shortage — no node currently has enough free CPU for the scheduler to place the pod — rather than a shortage of pod replicas.
Explicitly separates the two axes of responsibility: HPA only controls how many pod replicas exist; it has no mechanism or mandate to add new nodes/machines to the cluster.
Names the correct component for fixing this on a real cloud: Cluster Autoscaler (or Karpenter).

Explains at least the basic mechanism of how that component works on a real cloud — it watches for Pending pods caused by insufficient node resources and calls the cloud provider's API to add a node to the node group.
Explains specifically why this can't happen on a local `kind` cluster — kind's 'nodes' are just Docker containers on one host, so there is no real cloud provider API to call for more machines.

States a concrete practical consequence or takeaway for the kind lab — e.g. pods stay Pending until you delete the resource-hungry deployment or raise kind's Docker resource limits, and/or frames HPA and Cluster Autoscaler as complementary pod-axis vs node-axis mechanisms.

No — plain CPU-based HPA doesn't fit: a queue-reading worker is I/O-bound (spends time waiting on messages, not burning CPU), so even with a huge backlog CPU stays low and HPA sees no reason to scale up.
Plain HPA requires minReplicas >= 1 — it cannot scale a deployment down to 0 replicas, so "scale to 0 at night" is simply impossible with HPA regardless of metric.
The right tool is KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling), which ships scalers (Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, etc.) that read queue depth directly as the scaling signal instead of CPU.
KEDA activates the Deployment from 0 up to >=1 replicas as soon as the trigger (queue depth) becomes > 0 — this is the 0-to-1 jump plain HPA cannot do.
When the trigger returns to 0 and cooldownPeriod elapses with no new events, KEDA scales the Deployment back down to exactly 0.
From 1 replica upward, KEDA creates an underlying HPA (keda-hpa-...) that continues scaling using Kubernetes' standard ratio formula.

Trade-off to flag: scale-to-zero saves resources fully when idle, but the first message after a quiet spell pays a cold start — seconds to tens of seconds for KEDA to activate, schedule the pod, pull the image, and start the container.
If fast response is needed even when work is rare, use minReplicaCount: 1 or idleReplicaCount to keep a small warm floor instead of scaling fully to 0.

Missing `requests.cpu`: the container only declares `limits.cpu: 250m` with NO `requests.cpu` — CPU-based HPA computes `utilization = usage / requests.cpu`, so without `requests` there's no denominator, meaning `kubectl get hpa` will show `<unknown>/50%` forever and the HPA never scales no matter how correct `targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 50` looks. This is a dangerous silent bug because the manifest "looks valid" and `kubectl apply` reports no error.
Fix: declare `resources.requests.cpu` on the container (e.g. matching `limits.cpu: 250m`) so the HPA has a real usage baseline to compute utilization against.

`Deployment.spec.replicas: 3` is hardcoded while the same Deployment is already managed by an HPA — it may work initially, but the next time someone `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml`s it (e.g. from a CI/CD pipeline unaware of the HPA), the `replicas` field gets overwritten back to `3`, directly conflicting with what the HPA just set and causing a sudden, hard-to-debug replica jump.
Fix: `replicas` should be dropped entirely from the Deployment once an HPA manages it.

The HPA uses `apiVersion: autoscaling/v1` — the legacy version that only supports a single CPU metric via `targetCPUUtilizationPercentage`, with no multi-metric, custom/external metric support, and no `behavior` field to configure a stabilization window against thrashing.
Fix: bump to `autoscaling/v2` to be explicit and leave room for future extension (e.g. adding a request-per-pod custom metric).
Verify by running `kubectl get hpa web-cpu` and confirming it shows real TARGETS numbers instead of `<unknown>`.
Run a load test to confirm replicas actually scale with CPU once the fixes are applied.
